title: Quality planning and quality tolerances
blurb: Describe what quality planning produces, when it happens, how quality tolerances are set and how lower-level planning changes are handled.
question: Lower-level planning reveals that a product in the baselined PID needs to change. How should this be handled?

teach.body: Formally: quality planning is the capturing of quality specifications for the project's products and the generating of the associated product descriptions and the quality management approach. In plain English: agree how good each product must be, write it down product by product, and write one document explaining how the whole project will manage quality. It is the first of three quality elements, with quality control and quality assurance.

steps.sub: and acceptance criteria, in the PPD

teach.caption: The PPD comes from the user; the approach and product descriptions are the project's response.

items.label: QMA agreed; product descriptions for the project plan
Board approves the PPD and the QMA

teach.caption: Planning is not a one-off: product descriptions are refined as each stage is planned and run.

teach.body: The project product description should identify all the major products to be delivered. This matters because, when detailed product descriptions are written later, anything outside that coverage would be a requirement outside the approved scope. A complete PPD keeps product descriptions inside the boundary the board agreed.

Quality tolerance is the permissible deviation in a product's quality before escalation. Stakeholders prioritize their acceptance criteria and quality specifications, and these priorities are used to set the tolerances. A low-priority criterion can be given a wider range; a critical one, such as a safety level, may have little or none.

teach.caption: Illustrative figures. The point: the higher the priority, the tighter the tolerance.

teach.caption: Changes to the baselined PID arising from lower-level planning go through the issue management approach.

teach.h: Worked scenario: a health centre fit-out
teach.body: Westerby NHS Trust is fitting out a new clinic. In starting up, senior user Dr Ade Lawal states that rooms must meet infection control rules and be calm for patients. In initiation, project manager Sofia Marquez writes the quality management approach, referencing the trust's quality management system, and product descriptions for each room type. Infection control finishes get zero tolerance; paint colour gets a range. In stage two, detailed planning shows the X-ray room needs extra shielding, so Sofia raises it through the issue management approach.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) A change to the baselined PID found during lower-level planning is NOT just edited in; it goes through the issue management approach. (2) The user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria are captured in starting up, before the quality management approach is written in initiation. (3) Quality tolerances come from prioritized acceptance criteria and specifications, not from the risk budget.

items: Quality planning: capture quality specifications; produce product descriptions and the QMA.
PPD (from starting up) is a primary input; it should cover all major products.
QMA agreed in initiation and approved by the board.
Quality tolerances are set from prioritized acceptance criteria and quality specifications.
PID changes from lower-level planning go through the issue management approach.

summary: You can now describe what quality planning produces and when, and explain how quality tolerances are set. You can also say why the PPD must cover all major products and how changes found in lower-level planning are controlled.

A.q: Which outputs does quality planning produce?
options: Quality register entries and their related approval records
Product descriptions and the quality management approach
Highlight reports and checkpoint reports
The risk register and the issue register
A.why: Quality planning captures quality specifications for the products and generates the associated product descriptions and quality management approach (manual 8.2.1).

whyNot.0: Register entries and approval records are produced by quality control.
whyNot.2: Highlight and checkpoint reports belong to the progress practice.
whyNot.3: These registers belong to the risk and issues practices.

A.q: Why should the project product description identify all the major products?
options: To set the cost tolerance for each stage
To let teams start work before initiation
To keep later requirements inside the approved scope
To replace the need for separate product descriptions
A.why: Full coverage of the major products avoids requirements outside the approved scope being introduced when product descriptions are developed (manual 8.2.1.1).

whyNot.0: Stage cost tolerances are set by the project board, not through the PPD.
whyNot.1: Delivery work starts after the project is authorized.
whyNot.3: Product descriptions are still written for products; the PPD covers the project product.

A.q: How should changes to the baselined PID that arise from lower-level planning be handled?
options: By the team manager updating the PID
By recording them in the quality register
By waiting until the end project report
Through the issue management approach
A.why: Changes to the baselined PID arising from lower-level planning should be addressed using the issue management approach (manual 8.2.1.6).

whyNot.0: A baseline is changed under change control, not by a team manager editing it.
whyNot.1: The quality register records quality activities, not changes to the baseline.
whyNot.2: Changes must be controlled when found, not deferred to closure.

B.q:
Which two statements about quality planning are correct?
1. The PPD from starting up is a primary input to it.
2. It is carried out by the quality assurance function.
3. It results in product descriptions and the QMA.
4. It is completed once and not revisited.
options: 1 and 3
2 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 4
B.why: The expectations and acceptance criteria in the PPD are a primary input (1), and planning produces product descriptions and the QMA (3).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is false: quality assurance is an independent business function; planning is done within the project.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: product descriptions are developed or updated as stages are planned and run.
whyNot.3: Both are false: QA is independent of the project, and planning continues stage by stage.

B.q: A housing project rates 'meets fire regulations' as must-have and 'choice of door colours' as could-have. How should this affect the quality tolerances?
options: Both should get the same tolerance for fairness
The fire rating should get the wider tolerance
Tolerances should be set by the senior supplier
The fire rating should get little or no tolerance
B.why: Prioritized acceptance criteria and quality specifications are used to set quality tolerances, so a critical criterion gets a tight range.

whyNot.0: Tolerances follow priority, so different criteria can have different ranges.
whyNot.1: This reverses the logic: a must-have safety criterion needs the tightest range.
whyNot.2: Tolerances follow the users' priorities and are agreed through planning, not set by the supplier alone.

B.q: In which process are the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria first captured?
options: Initiating a project
Starting up a project
Controlling a stage
Managing a stage boundary
B.why: The expectations and acceptance criteria are documented in the project product description, produced in starting up a project.

whyNot.0: Initiation builds on them by agreeing the QMA and product descriptions.
whyNot.2: Controlling a stage applies quality planning to work packages; it does not first capture expectations.
whyNot.3: Stage boundaries update product descriptions for the next stage.

C.q: In which process is the quality management approach agreed, and who approves it?
options: Starting up a project; the senior user
Controlling a stage; the project manager
Initiating a project; the project board
Initiating a project; the quality assurance function
C.why: The QMA is agreed in initiating a project ('agree the management approaches') and approved by the project board in directing a project.

whyNot.0: Starting up captures expectations in the PPD; the QMA comes in initiation and the board approves it.
whyNot.1: The approach is in place before stages are controlled, and the PM does not approve it.
whyNot.3: Quality assurance is independent of the project and does not approve project management products.

C.q: From what are the management approaches, including the QMA, derived in initiation?
options: The highlight reports produced during the initiation stage
Business standards and users' expectations in the PPD
The team plans prepared by team managers
The end stage report from starting up
C.why: The approaches are derived from business strategies, standards or practices and from the users' quality and sustainability expectations captured in the PPD (manual 15.4.2).

whyNot.0: Highlight reports describe progress; they are not the source of approaches.
whyNot.2: Team plans are optional and come later, in managing product delivery.
whyNot.3: There is no end stage report for starting up; it is not a stage of the project.

C.q: During stage 2 planning, the project manager finds a product needs more detail and a requirement outside the PID scope. What is correct?
options: Update the product description; raise the new requirement as an issue
Leave the product description; add the requirement to the stage plan
Ask quality assurance to approve both changes directly
Record both in the quality register for the next review
C.why: Product descriptions are refined as stages are planned, but changes to the baselined PID arising from lower-level planning go through the issue management approach.

whyNot.1: Adding out-of-scope work straight into a plan bypasses change control.
whyNot.2: Quality assurance is independent of the project and does not authorize changes.
whyNot.3: The quality register records quality activities and results, not changes to scope.

reteach.title: Planning a wedding cake
reteach.question: What must be agreed before the baker starts?

blocks.h: Agree the standard, then the detail
blocks.body: The couple first say what they want overall: elegant and nut-free (expectations and criteria). The baker then writes how quality will be managed (tasting session, allergen checks, who signs off) and a spec for each tier. Nut-free has zero tolerance; the shade of icing can vary a little. If, while planning tier three, the couple want a fourth tier, that is a change to agree, not something added quietly.

blocks.text: A fourth tier found while planning tier three is a change to control, not a planning detail.

explain.body: Quality planning captures quality specifications and produces product descriptions and the quality management approach.

test.q: Which management product is produced by quality planning?
options: Quality register
Quality management approach
Exception report
Lessons report
test.why: Quality planning produces product descriptions and the quality management approach.

whyNot.0: The quality register records quality control activity.
whyNot.2: Exception reports belong to the progress practice.
whyNot.3: The lessons report passes lessons on; it is not a quality planning output.

explain.body: The PPD should name all major products so later product descriptions stay within the approved scope.

test.q: What risk does a PPD that misses a major product create?
options: Quality tolerances cannot be set
The executive cannot be appointed
Out-of-scope requirements creep in
The quality register cannot be opened
test.why: Coverage of all major products avoids introducing requirements outside the approved scope when product descriptions are written.

whyNot.0: Tolerances are still set from criteria and specifications.
whyNot.1: Appointing the executive is a starting up activity unrelated to PPD coverage.
whyNot.3: The register is set up in initiation whatever the PPD contains.

explain.body: Prioritized acceptance criteria and quality specifications are used to set quality tolerances.

test.q: What are quality tolerances based on?
options: The prioritized acceptance criteria and specifications
The highlight report frequency set by the board
The cost and time tolerances already set for the current stage
The supplier's standard contract terms
test.why: Prioritized acceptance criteria and quality specifications are used to set quality tolerances (manual 8.2.1.2).

whyNot.1: Report frequency is a progress control, not a basis for quality tolerance.
whyNot.2: Cost and time tolerances are separate aspects of performance.
whyNot.3: Contract terms are handled by the commercial management approach.

explain.body: When lower-level planning shows the baselined PID must change, use the issue management approach.

test.q: Which approach is used when lower-level planning requires a change to the baselined PID?
options: Quality management approach
Communication management approach
Risk management approach
Issue management approach
test.why: Changes to the baselined PID arising from lower-level planning are addressed using the issue management approach.

whyNot.0: The QMA covers quality techniques, standards and responsibilities, not change control.
whyNot.1: The communication management approach covers stakeholder communication.
whyNot.2: The risk management approach covers how risks are managed.
